notice: Hands-on labs, defined day by day. Every lab is LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT only: fictional data or isolated test systems, never production.

labs.title: Run a mini business impact analysis on a test service
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a fictional service or one you run in an isolated home or test lab. Do not interview colleagues or use production systems.
labs.goal: Practise turning business impact into MTD, RTO and RPO, and surface dependencies, before any recovery design.
prerequisites: Pick one fictional business process, for example 'agent cash-in for a mobile money service'
Cards: RTO, RPO, WRT, MTD; drill: RTO, RPO, MTD and WRT
steps: Describe the process in two sentences and name its owner.
List what it depends on: systems, data, people, suppliers, utilities, telecom links.
Estimate the impact of an outage at 1 hour, 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days: money, regulatory, reputation, safety.
Mark the point where impact becomes unacceptable: that is the MTD.
Estimate the work recovery time after a restore (checks, reconciliation) and set RTO = MTD − WRT or lower.
Set the RPO from how much data the process can lose and still be reconstructed.
Mark every single point of failure in the dependency list.
validation: RTO + WRT does not exceed MTD.
At least one external dependency is listed.
No recovery solution or vendor appears in the output: the BIA states requirements only.
rollback: Nothing to roll back: this is a paper exercise.
evidence: The completed impact table and the MTD, RTO, RPO line.
The list of single points of failure, ranked.

labs.title: Build a risk register for a fictional bank
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a new spreadsheet with fictional data only. Do not use real company risks, systems or names.
labs.goal: Turn a scenario into a working risk register with owners, ratings, treatments and an acceptance decision, and do one quantitative calculation.
prerequisites: A spreadsheet app (Excel, LibreOffice or Google Sheets)
Read the Mukuvisi Bank case study in Questions → Scenario sets
Cards: risk treatment, SLE/ARO/ALE, control types
steps: Create columns: ID, risk statement (threat + vulnerability + asset), owner, likelihood (1-5), impact (1-5), inherent score, existing controls, treatment, residual likelihood, residual impact, residual score, acceptance authority, review date.
Write five risks for the fictional Mukuvisi Bank, for example ransomware on core banking, stale policy, unclassified data, single telecom carrier, insider fraud in payments.
Score likelihood and impact for each and compute inherent score = likelihood × impact.
Choose a treatment for each (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and name one control per mitigated risk, labelled by type (preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating).
Re-score residual likelihood and impact after treatment and compute the residual score.
Set an appetite rule, for example residual 1-6 accepted by department head, 8-12 by executive, 15+ by board, and fill in the acceptance authority column.
For the ransomware risk, estimate asset value, exposure factor and annual rate of occurrence; compute SLE and ALE in a separate cell and compare with the annual cost of one control.
validation: Every risk names an owner from the business, not only IT.
Every risk has a treatment, a residual score and a review date.
Acceptance authority rises with residual score as your appetite rule says.
SLE = asset value × exposure factor and ALE = SLE × ARO are calculated correctly.
rollback: Nothing to roll back: the lab touches no system. Delete the spreadsheet if you do not want to keep it.
evidence: Export the register as PDF or a screenshot.
A three-sentence summary for the fictional board: top risk, recommended treatment, decision needed.

labs.title: Classify and mark a test file share
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a new folder of dummy files you create yourself. Do not use real company documents or shares.
labs.goal: Practise applying a classification scheme by impact, marking files so the label travels with them, and spotting over-classification.
prerequisites: A computer with a word processor and a spreadsheet app
Cards: who classifies, marking vs labelling
steps: Create a folder called LAB-share and 12 dummy files: for example a canteen menu, a press release, a staff phone list, a salary sheet, a board paper, a customer export, a draft contract, a published annual report, a password list (fake), a supplier price list, a patient list (fake names) and a project plan.
Write a four-level scheme with one line each: Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted, defined by the harm if disclosed.
For each file, write who the data owner would be in a real company and choose its level, with one sentence of reasoning.
Add a visible marking (header and footer) to every Confidential and Restricted file.
Add the level to each file's properties or metadata (for example the Tags or Keywords field).
Review your choices: move anything you rated higher than its real harm down a level, and note why.
Write one handling rule per level for storage, sending and destruction.
validation: Every file has an owner role and a level with a reason.
No more than a third of the files are at the top level; if more, you are over-classifying.
Confidential and Restricted files show the marking when printed or opened on another device.
Each level has storage, sending and destruction rules.
rollback: Delete the LAB-share folder. Nothing else is changed.
evidence: A table of file, owner role, level and reason.
A screenshot of one marked file and its metadata.

labs.title: See data remanence, then defeat it
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a spare USB stick or a virtual disk in a test VM that holds nothing you need. Never run recovery or wiping tools on a work device or a drive with real data.
labs.goal: Show that deleting and quick-formatting leave data recoverable, then sanitise the test media and show recovery fails.
prerequisites: A spare USB stick (8 GB or less is quickest) or a test VM with a second virtual disk
PhotoRec, the free open-source recovery tool from CGSecurity, downloaded from its official site
Card: clear, purge, destroy; drill: clear, purge, destroy
steps: Copy ten dummy files to the test media: a few photos you took yourself and some text files with a unique word such as LABMARKER in them.
Delete the files, empty the recycle bin and quick-format the media.
Run PhotoRec against the test media only, saving recovered files to a separate folder on your computer.
Count how many of the ten files came back, and search the recovered text files for LABMARKER.
Wipe the test media with a full overwrite (for example the operating system's full format, or a disk utility's zero-fill option).
Run PhotoRec again on the wiped media and count the recovered files.
Write two sentences on why this overwrite would not be enough for an SSD that held sensitive data.
validation: After the quick format, at least some files were recovered.
After the full overwrite, no LABMARKER files were recovered from the test media.
Your note mentions wear levelling or spare blocks, and names purge methods for SSDs (sanitise command or cryptographic erase).
rollback: Delete the recovered-files folder from your computer.
Reformat the test media for normal use, or delete the test VM's extra disk.
evidence: Screenshots of the PhotoRec results before and after the wipe.
Your counts and the two-sentence SSD note.

labs.title: Hashes vs signatures: tamper with a file and watch them fail
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a lab folder with dummy files you create. Do not sign real documents with lab keys.
labs.goal: Show that a hash detects change but proves nothing about who made the file, while a signature shows both integrity and origin.
prerequisites: Drill: symmetric vs asymmetric vs hashing
steps: Create a dummy file: `echo "Pay supplier 100" > order.txt`
Hash it: `openssl dgst -sha256 order.txt` and keep the digest.
Create a signing key pair: `openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out sign.key`, then `openssl pkey -in sign.key -pubout -out sign.pub`
Sign the file: `openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey sign.key -rawin -in order.txt -out order.sig`
Verify it: `openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey sign.pub -rawin -in order.txt -sigfile order.sig` (expect success).
Change 100 to 900 in order.txt, then repeat the hash and the verify; note what changed.
Write down why an attacker who changes the file can also publish a new matching hash, but cannot produce a valid signature without sign.key.
validation: The hash changes after editing the file.
Signature verification succeeds before the edit and fails after it.
Your note explains that a hash alone gives integrity but not origin.
rollback: Delete the LAB-sign folder, including sign.key.
evidence: The two digests and the two verify results.

labs.title: Build a two-tier test PKI and inspect certificates
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a test VM or a lab folder on a personal machine, using names ending in .test. Never use these certificates or keys on real services, and never install the lab root in a production trust store.
labs.goal: See how a certificate chain is built and verified, and what changes when the wrong CA or an expired certificate is used.
steps: Create a lab root CA: `openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -nodes -keyout root.key -out root.crt -days 30 -subj "/CN=LAB Root CA"`
Create a key and request for a server: `openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=portal.lab.test"`
Sign the request with the root: `openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA root.crt -CAkey root.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 7`
Verify the chain: `openssl verify -CAfile root.crt server.crt` (expect OK).
Inspect the certificate: `openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates` and note who issued it and when it expires.
Create a second, unrelated root (repeat step 1 with root2.key, root2.crt and CN=Other Root) and verify server.crt against root2.crt; note the error.
Write two sentences: what the root key's compromise would mean for every certificate it signed, and why real root keys live in HSMs.
validation: Verification succeeds against the lab root and fails against the unrelated root.
You can name the subject, issuer and validity dates of server.crt.
Your note mentions revoking and replacing everything the compromised root signed.
rollback: Delete the LAB-pki folder, including every .key file.
Nothing was installed into any trust store.
evidence: The output of both verify commands.
The subject, issuer and dates of server.crt.
